Fetched on demand by the detail page and read at build time by scripts/generate-prerender.mjs — NEVER imported into the JS bundle. Every fact here is standard NCERT/CBSE syllabus material; ncertRef names the chapter it comes from.

weathering-vs-erosion.ncertRef: NCERT Class 7 Geography, Chapter 3 — Our Changing Earth; extended in Class 9 and Class 11 Physical Geography.

paras: Weathering is the breaking down of rocks, soil and minerals where they already sit. The Latin root is the giveaway: it is the weather — rain, frost, heat, wind, dissolved gases — working on a rock face over years. Nothing is carried away. A boulder that cracks into six pieces but stays on the same hillside has been weathered, not eroded.

Because nothing moves, weathering is described as an in-situ (in place) process. It is the first stage in the long chain that turns solid bedrock into loose sediment and eventually into soil. Without weathering there would be no loose material for any other process to pick up, which is why every textbook treats it as the starting point.

Erosion is the removal and carrying away of that loosened material to somewhere else. It needs a transporting agent — running water, wind, moving ice or sea waves — and it always involves a change of place. The river that lifts weathered sand from a hillside and drops it 200 km downstream has eroded it.

Erosion is usually followed by transportation (the journey) and deposition (the drop-off). A delta at a river's mouth is made entirely of material that was weathered upstream, eroded, transported and finally deposited.
CBSE asks for these by name, so learn the type and one example of each.
bullets: Physical (mechanical) weathering — rock breaks apart without any change in its chemical make-up. Water seeps into a crack, freezes overnight, expands by about 9% and levers the crack wider; repeat this for a few winters and the rock splits. This is called frost wedging. In hot deserts, daily heating and night-time cooling makes the outer layer peel off in sheets — exfoliation.

Chemical weathering — the minerals themselves change into new substances. Rainwater dissolves carbon dioxide from the air to make weak carbonic acid, which slowly dissolves limestone; this is carbonation, and it is how limestone caves and the karst landscape of Meghalaya formed. Iron-bearing rocks turn reddish-brown as they react with oxygen and moisture — oxidation, the same chemistry as rust.

Biological weathering — living things do the work. Tree roots widen cracks as they thicken, lichens release acids that eat into rock surfaces, and burrowing animals expose fresh rock to air and water.

sections.h: The four agents of erosion and the landforms they leave
paras: Each agent leaves a signature set of landforms. Examiners frequently give you the landform and ask for the agent, so learn them as pairs.
bullets: Running water (rivers) — the most powerful agent overall. Erosional landforms: V-shaped valleys, gorges, waterfalls, meanders. Depositional landforms: floodplains, ox-bow lakes, levees and deltas. The Sundarbans delta is the classic Indian example.

Wind — dominant in deserts where there is no vegetation to hold the surface. It carves mushroom rocks (the base is worn faster because most sand is carried near the ground) and builds sand dunes and loess deposits.
Glaciers (moving ice) — grind out U-shaped valleys, cirques and hanging valleys, and dump unsorted debris as moraines. Seen across the Himalayas.
Sea waves — cut sea caves, which widen into sea arches, which collapse to leave sea stacks and steep sea cliffs.

paras: Weathering and erosion are sequential, not competing. The standard chain is: weathering breaks the rock → erosion picks the pieces up → transportation carries them → deposition drops them. Geographers group weathering, erosion and transportation together under one umbrella term, denudation, meaning the overall stripping-away of the land surface.

The practical consequence is that weathering can happen entirely on its own, but erosion cannot get started without material that has already been loosened. That asymmetry is the single most examined idea in this topic.

examples.t: A cracked rock on a Himalayan slope
examples.d: Water froze in the crack each night and split the rock. The pieces are still lying where they fell. Weathering only — no transport has happened.

examples.t: The Ganga carrying brown silt
examples.d: That silt was weathered off rocks upstream and is now being transported. This is erosion in progress; it will end as deposition in the Sundarbans delta.

examples.t: A rusty-red rock face in the Deccan
examples.d: Iron minerals have reacted with oxygen and moisture. Chemical weathering — the rock's composition itself has changed.

examples.t: A mushroom rock in the Thar Desert
examples.d: Wind-blown sand wore the base away faster than the top. Wind erosion, because the worn-off sand has been carried elsewhere.

mistakes: Writing that weathering 'moves' rock. It never does — the moment material is carried away, the process is erosion.
Treating erosion as the opposite of weathering. They are consecutive stages of one chain, not opposites.
Saying erosion causes weathering. It is the other way round: weathering supplies the loose material that erosion then removes.
Confusing erosion with deposition. Erosion is the picking-up and carrying; deposition is the dropping-off at the end of the journey.
Forgetting biological weathering. Many students list only physical and chemical and lose a mark.

quiz.q: A rock on a hillside splits into pieces after repeated freezing and thawing, but all the pieces remain in place. This is:
quiz.why: The rock broke down where it stood and nothing was carried away, which is the definition of weathering.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT an agent of erosion?
quiz.why: Temperature change breaks rock in place, so it is an agent of physical weathering. Erosion needs an agent that transports material.

quiz.q: Limestone caves are formed mainly by:
quiz.why: Rainwater with dissolved carbon dioxide forms weak carbonic acid, which dissolves limestone — carbonation, a chemical process.

quiz.q: The correct order of the denudation chain is:
quiz.why: Rock must first be broken down in place before any agent can remove, carry and finally drop it.

extraFaqs.q: Which happens first, weathering or erosion?
extraFaqs.a: Weathering happens first. It breaks the rock into loose fragments where they stand; only then can an agent such as water or wind pick those fragments up and carry them away, which is erosion.

extraFaqs.q: Is soil formation weathering or erosion?
extraFaqs.a: Soil formation begins with weathering. Rock is broken down in place into fine mineral particles, which then mix with decayed organic matter (humus) to become soil. Erosion actually removes topsoil, so it works against soil formation.

extraFaqs.q: Can erosion happen without weathering?
extraFaqs.a: Essentially no. Erosion needs loose material to carry, and weathering is what produces that loose material. The only partial exception is where an agent is powerful enough to pluck at solid rock directly, such as a fast river or a glacier, but even there weathering has usually weakened the rock first.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between erosion and deposition?
extraFaqs.a: Erosion is the removal and carrying away of material. Deposition is the dropping of that material when the transporting agent loses energy — a river slowing at its mouth, or wind dropping sand to build a dune.

paras: A physical map — also called a relief map — shows the natural features of the Earth's surface. Mountains, plateaus, plains, deserts, rivers, lakes and oceans all appear, and none of it depends on human decisions. If every border in the world were redrawn tomorrow, a physical map of India would look exactly the same.

Physical maps use a colour convention you are expected to know: green for plains and lowlands, yellow and brown for higher ground with darker browns for the highest mountains, blue for water bodies, and white for snow-covered peaks. That colouring is what lets you read height from a flat sheet of paper.

A political map shows features created by people and agreed by governments: country boundaries, state and district borders, capitals and major cities. Everything on it is a human decision, which means a political map can go out of date. India's political map changed when Telangana was formed in 2014 and again when Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh became separate Union Territories in 2019.

Political maps use a different convention: each state or country gets its own flat colour so neighbours are easy to tell apart, boundaries are drawn as distinct lines, and capitals are usually marked with a star or a circled dot.

sections.h: The three things every map must have
paras: Whatever its type, the NCERT syllabus says a map has three components. Questions on this come up almost every year.
bullets: Distance (scale) — the ratio between a distance on the map and the real distance on the ground. A scale of 1:50,000 means 1 cm on the map equals 50,000 cm, or half a kilometre, in reality.
Direction — shown by a north line or a compass rose. The four cardinal directions are north, south, east and west; north-east, south-east, south-west and north-west are the intermediate directions.
Symbols — standard signs and colours that let a small sheet carry a lot of information. Because symbols are internationally agreed, a map is readable even by someone who cannot read its language.

paras: Students often assume there are only two kinds of map, and lose marks for it. A thematic map shows one specific theme or piece of information — rainfall distribution, population density, road and rail networks, crop patterns, or forest cover.

Thematic maps are the ones you meet most often outside the classroom: a weather map on the news, a metro route map, an election results map. They may be drawn on top of either a physical or a political base.

sections.h: Map versus plan, and what scale changes
paras: A closely related distinction is between a map and a plan. A plan is a drawing of a very small area — a house, a school building, a plot of land — drawn to a large scale so that fine detail is visible. A map covers a much larger area at a smaller scale.

Scale is what makes this work. A large-scale map covers a small area with a lot of detail; a small-scale map covers a large area with little detail. A map of your town is large scale; a map of the whole world is small scale. The wording feels backwards to most students, which is exactly why it is examined.

examples.t: Finding the Western Ghats
examples.d: Use a physical map. Mountain ranges are natural features, shown in brown shading.

examples.t: Finding the capital of Rajasthan
examples.d: Use a political map. Capitals are human-designated and marked with a star.

examples.t: Finding where the monsoon brings most rain
examples.d: Use a thematic map — specifically a rainfall distribution map.

examples.t: Finding the route of the Godavari
examples.d: Use a physical map. Rivers are natural features, drawn in blue.

mistakes: Saying a physical map shows 'no cities at all'. Many physical maps do mark major cities for reference; the point is that its main purpose is natural features.
Forgetting thematic maps exist as a third category.
Mixing up large scale and small scale. Large scale = small area, more detail.
Writing that a political map never changes. It changes whenever boundaries are redrawn.
Confusing a plan with a map — a plan covers a very small area at a large scale.

quiz.q: Which map would you use to locate the Deccan Plateau?
quiz.why: A plateau is a natural landform, so it appears on a physical (relief) map.

quiz.q: On a physical map, brown usually represents:
quiz.why: The standard convention is green for plains, brown and yellow for higher ground, blue for water and white for snow.

quiz.q: A map showing the distribution of rainfall across India is a:
quiz.why: A map devoted to one specific theme, such as rainfall, is a thematic map.

quiz.q: A scale of 1:50,000 means 1 cm on the map equals:
quiz.why: 1 cm represents 50,000 cm on the ground. 50,000 cm = 500 m = half a kilometre.

extraFaqs.q: What are the three types of maps?
extraFaqs.a: Physical maps show natural features such as mountains, plateaus, plains and rivers. Political maps show human-made divisions such as countries, states, boundaries and capitals. Thematic maps show one particular theme, such as rainfall, population density or road networks.

extraFaqs.q: Why do political maps change but physical maps rarely do?
extraFaqs.a: Political maps record boundaries agreed by governments, and those decisions change — India's map changed when Telangana was created in 2014. Physical maps record natural features such as mountains and rivers, which change only over geological timescales.

extraFaqs.q: What are the three components of a map?
extraFaqs.a: Distance (shown by the scale), direction (shown by a north line or compass rose) and symbols (standard signs and colours). All three must be present for a map to be read correctly.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between a map and a globe?
extraFaqs.a: A globe is a true three-dimensional model of the Earth, so shapes and sizes stay accurate, but it cannot show small areas in detail and is awkward to carry. A map is flat, so some distortion is unavoidable, but it can show a small area in great detail and is easy to fold, print and compare.

evaporation-and-sublimation.ncertRef: NCERT Class 9 Science, Chapter 1 — Matter in Our Surroundings.

explainers.term: Evaporation: liquid to gas, from the surface only
paras: Evaporation is a liquid changing into vapour at temperatures below its boiling point. The key idea is that it happens only at the surface. Particles in a liquid move at a range of speeds; a few at the surface happen to be moving fast enough to escape the attraction of their neighbours and leave as vapour. This is why a puddle dries at 30 °C even though water boils at 100 °C.

Because the fastest particles are the ones that escape, the average energy of the particles left behind falls — and lower average energy means lower temperature. That is why evaporation causes cooling. It is why you feel cold stepping out of a swimming pool, why sweating cools you down, and why water stays cool in an earthen pot: water seeps through the pores, evaporates from the outside, and takes heat from the pot with it.

Sublimation is a solid changing directly into vapour without ever becoming a liquid. The liquid state is skipped entirely, and that single fact is the whole difference. Camphor left in a cupboard shrinks and disappears without ever leaving a puddle; naphthalene balls behave the same way.

The standard laboratory demonstration uses ammonium chloride heated in an inverted funnel over a china dish: the solid turns straight to vapour, rises, and re-forms as a solid on the cool glass above. Iodine and solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) also sublime — dry ice is named for exactly this reason, since it leaves no liquid behind.

sections.h: The four factors that speed up evaporation
paras: This list is examined directly almost every year. Learn all four with a reason for each.
bullets: Surface area — more exposed surface means more particles positioned to escape. Clothes spread out dry faster than clothes bundled up.
Temperature — heat gives particles more kinetic energy, so more of them can break free. Clothes dry faster in the sun.
Humidity — humidity is how much water vapour the air already holds. When the air is nearly saturated, evaporation slows. This is why clothes take so long to dry during the monsoon.
Wind speed — moving air carries away the vapour that has just formed, keeping the air above the liquid unsaturated so more can evaporate. Clothes dry faster on a breezy day.

sections.h: All six changes of state, and their names
paras: Naming the reverse processes correctly separates a full-mark answer from a partial one.
bullets: Melting (fusion) — solid to liquid, at the melting point.
Freezing (solidification) — liquid to solid, the reverse of melting.
Vaporisation — liquid to gas. This covers both evaporation (at the surface, any temperature) and boiling (throughout the liquid, at the boiling point only).
Condensation — gas to liquid, the reverse of vaporisation. Dew on grass, water droplets on a cold glass.
Sublimation — solid straight to gas.
Deposition (also called desublimation) — gas straight to solid, the reverse of sublimation. Frost forming on a cold window is water vapour depositing as ice.

paras: During a change of state, heat is absorbed or released but the temperature does not change. That hidden heat is called latent heat, and it goes into overcoming the forces holding the particles together rather than into raising temperature.

The latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg and the latent heat of vaporisation of water is 22.5 × 10⁵ J/kg. The vaporisation figure is far larger because the particles must be separated completely, not merely loosened. This is why steam at 100 °C causes a much worse burn than water at 100 °C: the steam releases all that extra latent heat as it condenses on your skin.

examples.t: Wet clothes drying on a line
examples.d: Evaporation. Liquid water at the fabric's surface becomes vapour well below 100 °C.

examples.t: A camphor tablet vanishing over a week
examples.d: Sublimation. The solid became vapour directly — the shelf underneath stayed dry.

examples.t: Feeling cold after a swim
examples.d: Evaporation causes cooling. The fastest water particles leave your skin, taking energy with them.

examples.t: Dry ice producing white fog
examples.d: Sublimation. Solid carbon dioxide becomes gas directly; the visible fog is water vapour from the air condensing in the cold.

examples.t: Frost on a windowpane
examples.d: Deposition — the reverse of sublimation. Water vapour becomes solid ice without becoming liquid first.

mistakes: Saying sublimation is 'fast evaporation'. They start from different states entirely — sublimation starts from a solid, evaporation from a liquid.
Claiming evaporation only happens at the boiling point. It happens at all temperatures, because it only needs surface particles with enough energy.
Confusing evaporation with boiling. Evaporation is a surface phenomenon at any temperature; boiling happens throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature.
Forgetting that evaporation causes cooling, and forgetting to explain why (the higher-energy particles leave).
Naming the reverse of sublimation as 'condensation'. Gas to solid is deposition; condensation is gas to liquid.

quiz.q: Camphor left in the open disappears without leaving any liquid. This is:
quiz.why: The solid turned straight into vapour with no liquid stage — the definition of sublimation.

quiz.q: Which of these does NOT increase the rate of evaporation?
quiz.why: Higher humidity means the air already holds a lot of water vapour, which slows evaporation down.

quiz.q: Water in an earthen pot stays cool because:
options: Water evaporates through the pores and takes heat with it
quiz.why: Water seeps through the porous clay and evaporates from the surface; the escaping high-energy particles carry heat away, cooling what remains.

quiz.q: The change of a gas directly into a solid is called:
quiz.why: Gas to solid is deposition (desublimation). Sublimation is the opposite direction, solid to gas.

extraFaqs.q: Why does evaporation cause cooling?
extraFaqs.a: Only the fastest-moving particles at the surface have enough energy to escape as vapour. When they leave, the average energy of the particles remaining is lower — and lower average kinetic energy means a lower temperature. The energy needed to escape is drawn from the liquid and its surroundings.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between evaporation and boiling?
extraFaqs.a: Evaporation happens only at the surface of a liquid and at any temperature below boiling point. Boiling happens throughout the whole liquid, forming bubbles, and only at one fixed temperature — the boiling point (100 °C for water at normal pressure).

extraFaqs.q: Give three substances that sublime.
extraFaqs.a: Camphor, naphthalene (mothballs), ammonium chloride, iodine and solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) all sublime. Ammonium chloride is the one usually used in the school laboratory demonstration.

extraFaqs.q: Why does steam at 100 °C burn more badly than water at 100 °C?
extraFaqs.a: Steam carries an extra 22.5 × 10⁵ J/kg of latent heat of vaporisation. When it touches skin it condenses and releases all of that energy on top of the heat from its temperature, so the burn is far more severe.

equator-and-prime-meridian.ncertRef: NCERT Class 6 Geography, Chapter 2 — Globe: Latitudes and Longitudes.

explainers.term: The Equator — the 0° line of latitude
paras: The Equator is an imaginary circle drawn around the Earth exactly midway between the North and South Poles. It is labelled 0° latitude, and it divides the globe into the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere.

It is the longest of all the parallels of latitude, roughly 40,075 km around, because it sits at the widest part of the Earth. Every other parallel is shorter, shrinking to a single point at each pole. The Equator is a real physical reference: the Sun is overhead there twice a year, at the equinoxes, and countries on it have almost equal day and night all year round.

explainers.term: The Prime Meridian — the 0° line of longitude
paras: The Prime Meridian is the semicircle of longitude that runs from the North Pole to the South Pole through Greenwich, near London. It is labelled 0° longitude and divides the globe into the Eastern Hemisphere and the Western Hemisphere.

Unlike the Equator, its position is a human choice, not a natural one. There is nothing physically special about Greenwich; an international conference in 1884 simply agreed to put zero there, and the world's clocks have been set from it ever since. Any meridian could have been chosen — and before 1884, different countries used different ones.

sections.h: Parallels of latitude — the important ones
paras: There are 181 parallels in total: 90 north, 90 south, and the Equator itself. Five carry names, and CBSE expects all five with their values.
bullets: Equator — 0°, the reference line.
Tropic of Cancer — 23½° N. Passes through eight Indian states, which is a favourite exam question.
Tropic of Capricorn — 23½° S.
Arctic Circle — 66½° N.
Antarctic Circle — 66½° S.

These lines mark the heat zones: the Torrid Zone between the two Tropics (the Sun is overhead here at some point in the year), the two Temperate Zones between each Tropic and its Circle, and the two Frigid Zones beyond the Circles.

sections.h: Meridians of longitude and the link to time
paras: There are 360 meridians — 180 east and 180 west of the Prime Meridian. Unlike parallels, all meridians are the same length and all of them meet at the two poles, which is why they are semicircles rather than circles.
Longitude and time are directly connected. The Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours, so it turns 15° in one hour and 1° in four minutes. Moving east, local time runs ahead; moving west, it falls behind.

India's Standard Meridian is 82°30′ E, passing through Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh. Because 82.5 × 4 minutes = 330 minutes, Indian Standard Time is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich Mean Time. The 180° meridian is the International Date Line, where the date changes by one day.

sections.h: The clean way to keep them straight
paras: Latitude lines run east-west but measure how far north or south you are. Longitude lines run north-south but measure how far east or west you are. Students reverse this constantly.

A memory hook that works: latitude sounds like 'ladder' — the rungs are horizontal and you climb them north or south. Longitude lines are 'long' — they run the long way, pole to pole. Together, a latitude and a longitude give a unique address for any point on Earth: Delhi is roughly 28.6° N, 77.2° E.

examples.t: A place at 0° latitude, 0° longitude
examples.d: The single point where the Equator meets the Prime Meridian, in the Gulf of Guinea off West Africa.

examples.t: Working out IST
examples.d: 82°30′ E × 4 minutes per degree = 330 minutes = 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT.

examples.t: Why Arunachal Pradesh sees sunrise before Gujarat
examples.d: Arunachal is further east. The Earth rotates west to east, so eastern longitudes meet the Sun first — about two hours earlier across India's width.

examples.t: The Tropic of Cancer in India
examples.d: 23½° N cuts across the middle of the country, passing through eight states including Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal and Mizoram.

mistakes: Calling the Prime Meridian a full circle. It is a semicircle from pole to pole; the Equator is the full circle.
Saying all parallels are equal in length. Only meridians are equal; parallels shrink towards the poles.
Writing that the Equator divides the Earth into east and west. It divides north and south — the Prime Meridian does east and west.
Forgetting that 1° of longitude equals 4 minutes of time, which is needed for every IST calculation.
Giving India's Standard Meridian as 82° E. It is 82°30′ E — the half degree is what makes IST 5:30 rather than 5:28.

quiz.q: The Equator divides the Earth into:
quiz.why: The Equator runs east-west at 0° latitude, separating the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. East and west are divided by the Prime Meridian.

quiz.q: India's Standard Meridian is:
quiz.why: 82°30′ E passes through Mirzapur; multiplying 82.5 by 4 minutes gives IST as GMT + 5:30.

quiz.q: How many parallels of latitude are there in total?
quiz.why: 90 in the Northern Hemisphere, 90 in the Southern, plus the Equator itself makes 181.

quiz.q: The Earth rotates through 1° of longitude in:
quiz.why: 360° in 24 hours is 15° per hour, so 1° takes 60 ÷ 15 = 4 minutes.

extraFaqs.q: Why was Greenwich chosen for the Prime Meridian?
extraFaqs.a: It was an international agreement, not a natural fact. At an 1884 conference the world agreed to place 0° longitude at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, largely because British nautical charts were already the most widely used. Any meridian could have been chosen instead.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between latitude and longitude?
extraFaqs.a: Latitude measures distance north or south of the Equator, and its lines run east-west as parallels of unequal length. Longitude measures distance east or west of the Prime Meridian, and its lines run north-south as semicircles of equal length that meet at the poles.

extraFaqs.q: What is the International Date Line?
extraFaqs.a: It is roughly the 180° meridian, on the opposite side of the globe from the Prime Meridian. Crossing it changes the calendar date by one day. It bends in places so that island groups and countries are not split across two different dates.

extraFaqs.q: Why is Indian Standard Time 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT?
extraFaqs.a: India's Standard Meridian is 82°30′ E. Since the Earth turns 1° every 4 minutes, 82.5° × 4 = 330 minutes, which is 5 hours 30 minutes. A single standard meridian is used so the whole country keeps one time.

square-and-cube.ncertRef: NCERT Class 8 Maths, Chapter 6 — Squares and Square Roots and Chapter 7 — Cubes and Cube Roots; shapes covered in Class 8 Chapter 10 — Visualising Solid Shapes.

explainers.term: This question has two different answers — check which one you need
paras: 'Difference between square and cube' is asked in two quite separate senses, and answering the wrong one loses full marks. The first sense is arithmetic: squaring a number versus cubing it. The second is geometric: the square as a flat 2D shape versus the cube as a 3D solid.

Both are on the CBSE syllabus and both are covered below. If the question mentions numbers, roots or exponents, it is the arithmetic sense. If it mentions faces, edges, vertices, area or volume, it is the shape sense.

explainers.term: Sense 1 — squaring versus cubing a number
paras: The square of a number is that number multiplied by itself once: n² = n × n. So 5² = 25. The cube is the number multiplied by itself twice more: n³ = n × n × n. So 5³ = 125.

The exponent is the only difference in the formula, but the growth rates diverge fast. For n = 10, the square is 100 and the cube is 1,000. For n = 20, the square is 400 and the cube is 8,000 — twenty times larger. This is why volume grows so much faster than area when an object is scaled up.

explainers.term: Sense 2 — the square shape versus the cube solid
paras: A square is a two-dimensional (flat) shape with four equal sides and four right angles. It has length and breadth but no thickness, so it has area but no volume.

A cube is a three-dimensional solid built from six identical square faces. It has length, breadth and height, so it has both surface area and volume. A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. In effect, a square is one face of a cube — the cube is what you get when a square is given depth.

sections.h: The formulas you need for both
paras: Learn these as pairs; questions very often ask for one of each.
bullets: Square of a number: n² = n × n. Square root: √n, the number which when squared gives n.
Cube of a number: n³ = n × n × n. Cube root: ∛n, the number which when cubed gives n.
Square shape, side a: Area = a², Perimeter = 4a, Diagonal = a√2.
Cube solid, edge a: Volume = a³, Total surface area = 6a², Lateral surface area = 4a², Space diagonal = a√3.

sections.h: Properties of square numbers that save time in exams
paras: These let you reject wrong options instantly in an MCQ, without calculating.
bullets: A perfect square never ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8. If a number ends in one of those digits, it cannot be a perfect square.
A perfect square never has an odd number of zeros at the end. 100 is a perfect square; 1000 is not.
The square of an even number is even; the square of an odd number is odd.
Squares are never negative. Cubes can be — (−4)³ = −64, while (−4)² = +16. This sign behaviour is the most examined difference between the two operations.
The sum of the first n odd numbers equals n². For example 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 = 4².

sections.h: Perfect squares and perfect cubes to memorise
paras: Notice that 1 and 64 appear in both lists — they are both perfect squares and perfect cubes (64 = 8² = 4³). The next such number is 729 = 27² = 9³.

examples.t: Square and cube of 7
examples.d: 7² = 49. 7³ = 343. The cube is seven times the square, which is always true: n³ = n² × n.

examples.t: A square tile of side 5 cm
examples.d: Area = 5² = 25 cm². Perimeter = 4 × 5 = 20 cm. There is no volume — the tile is treated as flat.

examples.t: A cubical box of edge 5 cm
examples.d: Volume = 5³ = 125 cm³. Total surface area = 6 × 5² = 150 cm². It has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.

examples.t: Why sign matters
examples.d: (−3)² = 9, but (−3)³ = −27. Squaring destroys the negative sign; cubing keeps it.

mistakes: Answering only the number sense when the question meant the shapes, or vice versa. Read the question for the words 'faces', 'volume' or 'area'.
Writing the total surface area of a cube as 4a². That is the lateral surface area; the total is 6a² because a cube has six faces.
Assuming a cube is 'a square in 3D' and therefore has 4 faces. It has 6.
Thinking a cube of a negative number is positive. Only even powers force a positive result.
Mixing up a cube (all edges equal) with a cuboid (a box whose length, breadth and height can differ).

quiz.q: What is the cube of 6?
quiz.why: 6³ = 6 × 6 × 6 = 216. 36 is the square, and 1296 is 6⁴.

quiz.q: How many edges does a cube have?
quiz.why: A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.

quiz.q: Which of these cannot be a perfect square?
quiz.why: 128 ends in 8, and no perfect square ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8.

quiz.q: The total surface area of a cube of edge 4 cm is:
quiz.why: Total surface area = 6a² = 6 × 16 = 96 cm². 64 cm³ would be its volume.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between a square and a cube?
extraFaqs.a: In arithmetic, the square of a number multiplies it by itself once (n² = n × n) while the cube multiplies it by itself twice more (n³ = n × n × n). In geometry, a square is a flat 2D shape with four equal sides and only area, while a cube is a 3D solid made of six square faces with both surface area and volume.

extraFaqs.q: Is a cube made of squares?
extraFaqs.a: Yes. A cube is bounded by six identical square faces. That is why its total surface area is 6a² — six squares, each of area a².

extraFaqs.q: Can a number be both a perfect square and a perfect cube?
extraFaqs.a: Yes. Such numbers are perfect sixth powers. The first few are 1, 64 (which is 8² and 4³) and 729 (which is 27² and 9³).

extraFaqs.q: Why is the cube of a negative number negative?
extraFaqs.a: Cubing multiplies three negative factors together. Two negatives give a positive, and the third negative makes the result negative again. Squaring uses only two factors, so the negatives always cancel and the answer is positive.
